purpose: Published throughput figures for predicting how slow a grounded question would be on hardware nobody here has.
how_to_read_this: Every row is a figure somebody else measured and published, not a figure measured here. Each one names the page it came from and the day it was read off that page.

A row is 'estimated' because it describes hardware this project has never run on. It becomes 'measured' only for the machine that runs 'archiv model calibrate --local', and that measurement is written into the archive, never back into this file.

Prompt processing and generation are kept apart on purpose. Archiv's workload is prompt-heavy -- roughly eight passages plus an instruction block against a few hundred tokens of reply -- so on a processor without a graphics card the wait is almost all before the first word appears. A single 'tokens per second' number hides that completely.

The band on each figure is the spread the source itself reported. Where a source published one number with no spread, the band is that number twice and says so. That is not a range; it is one observation, and a reader should treat it as one.
what_this_table_does_not_contain: Memory bandwidth. The prediction code can derive a second, independent throughput ceiling from a machine's memory bandwidth and the size of the model file, and that arithmetic is implemented and tested. No row carries a bandwidth figure, because the vendor pages that publish them are unreachable from the environment this table was built in, and a bandwidth number recalled from memory is not a cited number. Until a row has one, its prediction rests on one anchor and says so.

Any figure for Archiv's own prompt sizes. Every source below benchmarks a 512-token prompt because that is what the standard harness does. Archiv's prompts are larger, and prompt processing is not perfectly linear in prompt length, so these figures are an anchor rather than a direct answer.
